title: Administrative hearsay, subpoenas, and substantial evidence
shortTitle: Administrative hearsay, subpoenas, and substantial evidence
summary: Admissibility of hearsay and sufficiency of evidence are separate questions, assessed with reliability and the opportunity to challenge adverse material.
notes:
Administrative hearings may receive relevant oral and documentary evidence even when courtroom hearsay rules would exclude it. That permission does not itself establish that the resulting record adequately supports an adverse decision. Perales allows reliable medical reports to contribute substantial evidence under conditions that included examination by specialists, corroboration, access to the reports, and an unused opportunity to request subpoenas. Its disposition still required a judicial assessment of the whole admissible record.

The notes identify reliability factors such as contrary direct testimony, the form and source of the statement, internal indicia of accuracy, and corroboration. They also note Biestek’s rejection of a categorical rule that an expert’s refusal to provide private market data automatically prevents the testimony from constituting substantial evidence. Finally, the subpoena regulation permits issuance when reasonably necessary for full presentation; courts commonly review that determination as discretionary. A party’s ability to request a subpoena and an absolute entitlement to receive one are different propositions.
